rationale.intervention_reconstruction: The hypothesis proposes adding Ti and C to form TiC precipitates via spark plasma sintering, whereas the paper studied an as-cast equimolar WTaTiVZr alloy made by arc melting without intentional carbide formation. This is a different kind of intervention (precipitation engineering vs. multicomponent solid-solution alloying).
rationale.condition_agreement: The hypothesis specifies high-temperature testing at or above 1000 °C under high heat flux, while the paper used room-temperature compression, indentation from 25–500 °C, and room-temperature scratch testing. These are entirely different regimes.
rationale.mechanism_agreement: The hypothesis invokes strengthening and toughening via nanoscale TiC precipitates acting as dislocation barriers and bridging interfaces. The paper attributes properties to solid-solution strengthening, lattice distortion, and effects of Ti, V, Zr on dislocation cores and grain-boundary cohesion, with no precipitate-mediated mechanism. These are different classes of mechanism.
rationale.outcome_agreement: The hypothesis predicts improved high-temperature plasticity and toughness relative to a baseline without TiC. The paper reports improved room- and moderate-temperature strength, plasticity, and toughness for the HEA relative to pure tungsten, but the property direction is only generally aligned and the temperature regimes differ completely.
